title: Binstack: Choosing the single most impactful option with binary materiality and stack-ranked attributes
summary: Jason Cohen argues that weighted rubrics fail for multi-dimensional decisions because scores are imprecise, incomparable and tie easily. His Binstack method replaces scores with binary "material or not" judgments against a stack-ranked list of attributes, producing a clear winner and an easy-to-explain decision.

principles.text: Weighted-score rubrics produce ties and noise; differences in totals are more error than signal.
principles.quote: Even with weights, a clear winner often does not emerge, and again we're back to a weak, indefensible decision.

principles.text: Summing incomparable attributes implicitly claims they are interchangeable, which sounds absurd when said aloud.
principles.quote: By adding them together, we're implicitly saying "these are comparable," but they are not.

principles.text: Score each option as binary materiality: it either moves an attribute by a measurable amount or it doesn't. Write the concrete expected change down.
principles.quote: Either an item *materially* contributes to that attribute, or it doesn't. "Materially" means the effect is so large you can measure it easily

principles.text: Hard decisions are hard because smaller decisions were avoided. Decide what matters by ordering attributes in a single ranked list.
principles.quote: A general rule of complex decisions, is that often they're difficult because we've avoided making other, smaller decisions.

principles.text: Filter candidates attribute by attribute from the top rank down; the first option left alone on an attribute wins.
principles.quote: Cross out items that don't materially address the top-ranked attribute.

principles.text: A good decision must be explainable, including why rejected options lost; involving the proposer makes rejection easier to accept.
principles.quote: Not only do you need the best decision, you also need to be able to **explain your decision to others**, especially to those who wish the decision had gone a different way.
